attribution.note: Zitron's own conclusion in his newsletter, drawn from the Ramp data he cites.

semantics.note: The proposition matches the firm present-tense claim. The aside about where software money sits is rightly treated as context.

contract.note: Reading 'not much money' as modest relative to company size or software budget is an ordinary plain reading. Neither 'vast majority' nor 'much' has a threshold, so the result depends on the evaluator's reading.

evidence.note: Ramp's July median of about $12 per employee fits modest spending at a typical sampled firm. But it covers only Ramp's sample and says nothing about how much the upper half spends.
Measures adoption and plans to spend more, not actual spending. The contract excludes intentions as a substitute for expenditure, so this neither supports nor contradicts.

reviews.rationale: The Ramp median is consistent with modest typical spending, but the packet has no representative distribution showing that a vast majority of enterprises spend modestly relative to size or budget. The Morning Consult survey covers intentions only. The evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion, restating his earlier analysis in his own words.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the >70% share and the list of providers. It leaves out 'direct contracts or via hyperscalers', but the contract includes it.

contract.note: Measuring realized AI revenue is reasonable. However, the speaker never said whether the share applies to each provider or to the group pooled. The contract lets one provider at or below 70% contradict the claim, so the result could turn on that choice.

evidence.note: The Cerebras filing shows OpenAI dominates its future obligations and gives OpenAI revenue for Q2. It gives no AI revenue denominator and no Anthropic or indirect revenue, so it cannot test the 70% share.

reviews.rationale: The only usable evidence is partial data for one of the seven named providers. Nothing in the packet establishes AI revenue shares for Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle, SpaceX, or Lambda, and nothing gives a complete share for Cerebras. The claim cannot be settled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own estimate, presented as the result of his own analysis.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the estimate framing and his concession that the figure could be smaller. That concession widens the tolerance downward, so a lower true figure fits his words better than a higher one.

contract.note: Treating the figure as an approximate annual purchasing pace, with NVIDIA plus Jane Street above half and NVIDIA larger, is a fair reading. The contradiction test should take account of the downward concession.

evidence.note: CoreWeave's own announcement of a roughly $6B Jane Street commitment. It has no annual schedule and no market total.

NVIDIA's 10-Q lists $36B of AI cloud commitments over several years, falling as third parties use the capacity. It does not give NVIDIA's actual annual purchases, so it does not contradict the estimate.
Ramp describes GPU purchasing structures and admits limited visibility into demand. It offers no market total and no breakdown by buyer.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows Jane Street and NVIDIA buy compute but gives no reconciled annual total of compute demand excluding OpenAI and Anthropic, and no buyer shares. NVIDIA's multiyear commitments cannot be converted into annual spending. The evidence neither supports nor contradicts the roughly $22B estimate.

attribution.note: Zitron's own closing prediction in the essay.

semantics.note: Only 'will lead to a market correction' is firm. The size claim ('likely dwarfs the Dot Com Bubble') is hedged with 'likely'. The insults are rhetoric.

contract.note: The contract's test hinges on whether the correction dwarfs the dot-com bust, which the speaker hedged with 'likely'. Policy bars scoring hedged language on a plain reading. The firm remainder, a correction of some size with no deadline, is undefined.

evidence.note: ECB blog on boom-bust risk in general. It shows no correction happening.
Reports an AI-related one-day sell-off on Oct 22. That is not a completed correction, there is no comparison with the dot-com bust, and no evidence on cause.

reviews.rationale: The size prediction is hedged with 'likely', so it is not scored. The firm part, that the failures will lead to some market correction, has no deadline, and no conclusive event appears in the evidence. A single-day sell-off does not settle it. Nothing scorable can be assessed.
